text:
Guinea is seeking backing from US, Chinese and multilateral financiers for a planned $1.9 billion deep-water port, its mines minister told Reuters, aiming to build on the giant Simandou iron ore project and turn the country into a regional trade hub.
The project would be among Africa’s largest, and marks Guinea’s latest effort to leverage its vast mineral wealth following the launch of the Simandou project and comes as governments and investors compete for influence over infrastructure supporting global mineral supply chains.
Mines Minister Bouna Sylla said the government had completed feasibility studies and was engaging a broad group of potential financiers, including the US International Development Finance Corporation, Chinese investors, the World Bank, the African Development Bank, Africa Finance Corporation and the International Finance Corporation.
He did not provide a timeline for selecting investors or starting construction of the project, which has a planned 20-metre draft capable of handling 200,000-metric-ton Capesize vessels.
The port would be Guinea’s biggest infrastructure project since Simandou, the roughly $20 billion iron ore development that shipped its first output last year after decades of delays. The project, jointly developed by Rio Tinto (LON: RIO), (ASX: RIO), China’s Baowu Steel and other partners, includes a 600-kilometre (373-mile) railway and deep-water export terminal.
While Simandou’s infrastructure was designed primarily to transport iron ore from one of the world’s largest untapped deposits, the proposed port is intended as a multi-user facility serving miners, container traffic and industrial operators, Sylla said, reflecting Guinea’s broader goal of converting its mineral wealth into a platform for trade.
“Simandou has shown the importance of large-scale infrastructure,” he said. “Our objective now is to develop infrastructure that can support mining, trade and industrial development on a much broader scale.”
Guinea, the world’s largest bauxite producer, has largely seen mining companies build dedicated railways and export terminals tailored to individual projects.
The new port would mark a shift towards shared infrastructure that could also serve other industries and regional users.
Sylla said the project’s economics should make it a compelling alternative to bauxite miners’ dedicated rail and port facilities.
“It is a port for everyone,” he said. “We want to diversify the sources of funding rather than rely on a single source.”
(Reporting by Maxwell Akalaare Adombila; Editing by Clara Denina and Louise Heavens)
